14579: The Rapture and the Return of Christ
14580: When is the church gathered to Christ?
14581:
Paul tells the Thessalonians that when the Lord descends from heaven, the dead in Christ will rise first and living believers will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air (1 Thess 4:16-17). The Latin Vulgate's verb for caught up, rapiemur, gives the English word rapture. That believers will be gathered to Christ at his coming is stated in the text; the debated question is when this gathering happens relative to a final period of tribulation and to Christ's visible return.

Within premillennialism, pretribulationists place the rapture before a seven-year tribulation, midtribulationists at its midpoint, prewrath advocates partway through the second half before God's wrath is poured out, and posttribulationists at the end, as part of the single visible return. Amillennialists, postmillennialists and preterists generally see no separate rapture at all: 1 Thessalonians 4 describes the one second coming.

A related historical question is whether a pretribulation rapture was taught before John Nelson Darby in the 1830s. Several earlier texts have been proposed, and each is debated.
14583:
Pretribulationism teaches that Christ will come for his church before the seven-year tribulation (Daniel's seventieth week), raising dead believers and transforming living ones and taking them to heaven. After the tribulation, during which God deals especially with Israel and judges the world, Christ returns visibly with his saints to establish the millennial kingdom. The second coming therefore has two phases: the rapture (Christ for his saints, in the air) and the revelation (Christ with his saints, to the earth).

The view rests on the distinction between Israel and the church, on the conviction that the tribulation is entirely a period of divine wrath from which the church is exempt, and on the imminence of Christ's coming, meaning that no prophesied event must occur before the rapture. It is closely associated with dispensational premillennialism.
14585: Darby developed and spread the doctrine of a rapture before the tribulation as part of his distinction between the heavenly church and earthly Israel. Pretribulationists generally regard him as having recovered or systematized a biblical teaching; critics regard him as its originator. Whether earlier writers held it is debated.

14594:
Pretribulationism emerged among the Brethren in the 1830s within a revival of premillennial expectation in Britain. It spread to North America through Bible conferences, the Scofield Reference Bible and Bible institutes, becoming the most common view among American evangelicals and many Pentecostals in the twentieth century. It gained a vast popular audience through Hal Lindsey and the Left Behind novels and films.

The question of whether it was taught before Darby is contested: proponents point to Pseudo-Ephraem, Morgan Edwards and others; critics argue these sources are ambiguous, and some (notably Dave MacPherson) argued that it arose from Margaret MacDonald's 1830 vision, a claim most historians regard as unproven.

14649:
Midtribulationism holds that the church will be raptured at the midpoint of Daniel's seventieth week, three and a half years into the seven-year period. The first half contains the rise of antichrist and preliminary troubles caused largely by human wickedness, through which the church passes; the second half is the great tribulation and the outpouring of God's wrath, from which the church is removed.

Its best-known defender, Gleason Archer, called his view a mid-seventieth-week rapture to stress that the church is spared the wrath of the final three and a half years. Midtribulationists often identify the last trumpet of 1 Cor 15:52 with the seventh trumpet of Rev 11:15 and see the ascension of the two witnesses in Rev 11:11-12 as a picture of the rapture.
